findings.summary: The caption's first sentence is a series label, not a hook.
findings.fix: Open with the hook and move the part label after it: "One endpoint for clients, ten teams shipping independently — that is the whole pitch of GraphQL federation, and the bill arrives in round trips. Part 3 of GRAPHQL FEDERATION: how the router plans a query at runtime."

findings.summary: The page opens with leftover composition and publishing material, so the first thing under a query-planning title is ship-order rules and a hot-reload callout.
findings.evidence: page_title "Query Planning & The Router At Runtime" is followed first by heading "Order Of Operations" ("adding a field | deploy code, then publish schema") and callout "No Restart", and only then by "Plan, Then Execute"
findings.fix: Move the "Order Of Operations" table and "No Restart" callout to the end of the previous composition page, or give them their own composition/publish heading, so this page starts with "Plan, Then Execute".

findings.summary: The four plan nodes are listed but never shown working together, and the page never explains how later steps pass data along through `_entities` representations, so `Flatten` and `Sequence` stay abstract.
findings.evidence: Table rows "`Flatten` | path into the response" and "`Sequence` | ordered steps"; nothing mentions that later steps send `_entities` calls with representations taken from earlier responses, or that `@requires` forces `Sequence` while independent sibling branches become `Parallel`
findings.fix: After the node table, add a small example plan such as Fetch(accounts) → Flatten(me) → Fetch(reviews, `_entities`), plus a bullet saying that sibling branches with no data dependency run as `Parallel` and `@requires` forces `Sequence`.

findings.summary: One hashtag is misspelled, so it will not reach the intended API-architecture audience.
The callout says schema changes never need a router redeploy, but the router only picks up a new supergraph without a restart when hot reload or managed federation (Uplink) is enabled.
findings.evidence: "The router hot-reloads a new supergraph in place. Schema change never means a gateway redeploy"
findings.fix: Name the condition: "With managed federation (Uplink) or --hot-reload, the router swaps in a new supergraph in place, so a schema change doesn't need a gateway redeploy."

findings.summary: Calling query planning the expensive half of the router's job is misleading: plans are cached, and per-request latency usually comes from the subgraph fetches during execution.
findings.evidence: "It is the expensive half of the router's job"
findings.fix: Change to "Planning is CPU-heavy on a cold cache, which is why plans are cached; execution (subgraph round trips) usually dominates latency."

findings.summary: The entry-point rule sits under the caching heading even though it describes how a plan executes, not how plans are cached.
findings.evidence: Under heading "Plan Caching": "Step 1 always hits a subgraph owning a root field"
findings.fix: Move this bullet into the "Plan, Then Execute" section, next to the plan-node table and the new `_entities` follow-up-step bullet.

findings.summary: The caching table uses "APQ" and "entity cache" without defining either one.
findings.evidence: Table rows "APQ | request body size" and "entity cache | subgraph fetch"; the only related text is "Persisted queries shrink the request"
findings.fix: Spell out APQ as Automatic Persisted Queries (the client sends a hash instead of the full query text), and add a short note that an entity cache stores subgraph `_entities` results.

findings.summary: The claim that a failing non-null field propagates its null upward has no example, and a learner is unlikely to follow it without one.
findings.evidence: "a non-null field nulls its nearest nullable ancestor"
findings.fix: Add a one-line example, e.g. if `Product.price: Int!` fails in `topProducts: [Product]`, that whole `Product` becomes `null` in the list.
